Oct 26 : Shares of India's Infosys fell 2.7 per cent on Monday after the software exporter sharply cut its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast, underscoring challenges from AI-driven pricing pressure, tougher competition and sluggish demand in key markets. The firm was the last of the top 5 to report earnings for the Indian IT sector. Earlier this month, peers Tata Consultancy Services and HCLTech met revenue estimates with modest margin performance, but investors cheered the uptick in AI revenue. The company cut its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast to 1 per cent-2 per cent from 1.5 per cent-3 per cent, while most analysts had expected it to trim only the upper end of the range to 2.5 per cent. "Peers are better placed than Infosys at this point, and the share movement is just reflecting that. Infosys has been underperforming from Q4FY26 results," LKP Securities analyst Anshul Jethi said.

AI competition and clients expanding their global capability centres or offshore tech hubs directly, rather than engaging Infosys for IT services, are also hurting the company, he added. Systematix analysts called it a "disappointing quarter", highlighting pricing pressure from heightened competition and client productivity demands on account of AI, and subdued tech spending among retail and high-tech clients. Brokerage Motilal Oswal said weaker volumes, smaller-than-expected price increases, a shift toward offshore delivery and Infosys' decision to exit a large European manufacturing contract had weighed on growth. TD Cowen said macroeconomic uncertainty, AI-led productivity demands, and heightened competition have hurt pricing and volumes, while seasonal weakness and client ramp-downs could weigh on second-half growth. Analysts rate the stock "Buy" on average, with a median price target of 1,180 rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG. Shares were last trading 1.5 per cent lower at 1,136 rupees as of 10:53 a.m. IST. The Nifty IT index was down 0.2 per cent while the benchmark Nifty 50 index was up 0.16 per cent.

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 26 : The Bank of Japan will likely declare victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its 2 per cent inflation target at its policy meeting on Friday and emphasise the risks prices could overshoot, signaling the chance of a rate hike as soon as December. Such hawkish language may reinforce expectations the BOJ, US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank will all raise rates by year-end, as brisk AI demand and the Iran war-induced energy shock worsen global inflationary pressures. Still, the BOJ is likely to avoid dropping explicit hints on the timing and pace of future rate rises as it balances the need to forestall risks of an inflation overshoot without disrupting jittery markets with a premature hike, analysts say. "With rises in prices and wages moderate, the BOJ will keep raising rates gradually without rushing," said a person familiar with its thinking, a view echoed by two more people.

At the two-day policy meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ is set to maintain its policy rate at 1.25 per cent by a majority vote, forgoing a back-to-back hike to spend more time scrutinising the effect of past rate hikes on lending conditions. In a quarterly report due after the meeting, the BOJ is likely to slightly revise up next fiscal year's price forecast and signal that underlying inflation has roughly achieved its 2 per cent target, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters. With wage gains becoming embedded and inflation expectations hovering around 2 per cent, the central bank will likely stress that it will now focus on anchoring inflation around its target by raising rates toward levels deemed neutral to the economy. While Governor Kazuo Ueda has already signaled such a shift in policy focus upon raising rates in September, the pivot would mark another symbolic departure from the BOJ's prolonged efforts to fire up inflation through ultra-loose monetary policy. "It's a historical moment for the BOJ, though it faces a more challenging task now that it needs to step not just on the accelerator but the brakes," said Naomi Muguruma, chief bond strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities. "The BOJ will probably scrutinise upcoming data and market moves in deciding whether to raise rates in December, or hold until January," she said. Analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.5 per cent in December and stick to a quarterly pace of rate hikes. FUNDING STILL LOOSE Under former governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ deployed a massive stimulus in 2013 to pull Japan out of deflation and fire up inflation to its 2 per cent inflation target. Even after ending its mix of unorthodox easing steps in 2024, the central bank has trodden cautiously in raising rates on the view underlying inflation - or price moves excluding one-off factors and driven by domestic demand - remained below target. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. The BOJ's policy rate, at 1.25 per cent, is now within the range of 1.1 per cent to 2.5 per cent its staff estimated as Japan's neutral rate, or the level that neither cools nor overheats the economy - drawing market attention to how far it could eventually hike rates. With growth in bank lending still strong, the central bank is likely to stress on Friday that financial conditions remain loose - signalling scope for further rate hikes before its policy rate reaches levels close to neutral, the people said. The BOJ's meeting follows that of the Fed, which is seen skipping a hike at its two-day meeting concluding on Wednesday. The ECB is also set to keep rates unchanged at 2.5 per cent on Thursday.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SEOUL, Oct 26 : SK Hynix said it will announce shareholder return measures on Wednesday when the South Korean chipmaker releases quarterly results, responding to a report that it is considering a special dividend of about 16 trillion won ($12 billion). South Korean newspaper Dong-A Ilbo reported on Monday that SK Hynix is considering the special dividend, which will be funded by gains from selling its stake in Japanese memory chipmaker Kioxia. SK Hynix has not publicly disclosed details of the stake sale, which was completed earlier this year, and analysts estimate that it recognised hefty cumulative investment gains. SK Hynix invested about 4 trillion won in Kioxia in 2018 through a Bain Capital-led consortium of US, Japanese and South Korean investors.

When asked about the media report by the stock exchange operator, SK Hynix said that it is "reviewing various shareholder return measures" and plans to announce them alongside third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. It did not elaborate. Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have faced growing pressure from investors to return a bigger share of excess cash through dividends or share buybacks after record profits fuelled by booming demand for AI memory chips. The pressure increased especially after their shares plunged from record highs hit in June, partly on investor concerns over the durability of AI spending by US technology companies. SK Hynix shares firmed up 0.5 per cent, bucking the wider market that was down 1.3 per cent. In August, SK Hynix said it will buy back and cancel 40 trillion won of its own shares and allocate more than 50 per cent of free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027 to boost shareholder returns. SK Hynix said on Friday it paused a planned US listing for its Solidigm chip unit due to market volatility — a move which also comes after it faced concerns from investors and regulators about the potential listing that had weighed on its shares. TOKYO, Oct 26 : Japan's Nikkei share gauge lost ground for a third straight session on Monday as chip-related shares continued their decline, while energy-linked shares gained on higher oil prices. The benchmark Nikkei 225 slid 0.80 per cent to close at 62,189.65, its lowest closing level since July 30. The broader Topix edged up 0.18 per cent to 3,972.98. US share gauges ended lower on Friday, but the S&P 500 energy sector rose 2.5 per cent to a record. Oil prices slid from a six-month high on Monday after reports that Qatari mediators visited Tehran to seek de-escalation in coordination with the United States, following intensified Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia that had stoked supply concerns.  "The Nikkei Stock Average is showing signs of short-term technical undervaluation," Monex Securities senior analyst Satoshi Saito said in a note. "Stocks may see phases of short-term rebound, but with several concerns in the background, the recovery may remain sluggish for now."

GMO Internet Group said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorised access following an attack on its foreign exchange trading service. Its shares plunged 15.65 per cent, the sharpest decline since March 2011. Breadth was largely positive on the Nikkei, but the heavy weighting of tech shares dragged it lower. The gauge had 149 gainers and just 73 decliners. The largest losers were online retailer Mercari, down 6.21 per cent, followed by Screen Holdings, 4.34 per cent lower, and Kokusai Electric, which lost 4.29 per cent. The biggest winners were energy explorer Inpex, up 4.90 per cent, followed by internet security firm Trend Micro, 4.20 per cent higher, and Mitsubishi Corp, which gained 4.14 per cent.

FAST

SYDNEY, Oct 26 : Share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as oil eased from six-month highs ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and company earnings that will further test investor confidence in the AI boom. Brent oil slipped 1.0 per cent to $115.48 amid reports Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States. Brent futures jumped 6.2 per cent last week to their highest weekly close since mid-2022 as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over energy supplies. US crude futures fell 1.1 per cent to $102.08 a barrel. Japan's Nikkei dipped 0.8 per cent, after losing 4.0 per cent last week, while South Korea fell 0.4 per cent, having shed almost 19 per cent so far this month. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.

The inflationary pulse from oil is likely to alarm all the central banks meeting this week, with hikes seen as just a matter of time even if some hold for now. "The main message from global central banks grappling with this year's macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway," said Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan. "G3 central banks are likely to remain on hold, but Canada should start its tightening cycle and first moves are expected from the UK and Sweden next month." New Zealand's central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US Federal Reserve will stand pat, but imply an 80 per cent chance it will pull the trigger in December. Much the same is priced in for the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank. A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1 per cent in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2 per cent annualised pace thanks in part to furious spending on data centres. "The Fed is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," they added. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." HYPERSCALERS TO TEST AI HYPE On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both edged up 0.2 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.2 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.1 per cent.  Earnings highlights will include the hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, among one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting. Results from Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade. Consensus on Microsoft is for $90.6 billion of revenue and an adjusted EPS of $4.73, with Amazon at $202 billion of revenue and EPS around $1.97. Alphabet revenue is seen at $128 billion and EPS of $3.00. Equity valuations have been tested by higher bond yields, though Treasuries did manage a rally last week before running into renewed selling on Friday. Yields on 10-year Treasuries were at 5.0 per cent, but off a peak of 5.36 per cent hit early in the month. In currency markets, the Japanese yen retained its safe-haven appeal at 157.00 per dollar, having gained around 0.8 per cent last week. The euro held steady at $1.1204 as political unrest in France kept investors wary, though the country did escape a credit downgrade last week. Sterling held at $1.3346 with Britain's new finance minister, John Healey, set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war. The Brazilian real was yet to trade in Asia as Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold was a fraction firmer at $4,001 an ounce, having fallen more than 4 per cent last week. [GOL/]

Source: Reuters

BEIJING, Oct 26 : Oil prices fell on Monday after surging to near six-month highs late last week, although ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus. US crude futures were down $1.60, or 1.55 per cent, at $101.67 per barrel by 0018 GMT. Brent crude futures were down $1.56 or 1.34 per cent at $115.16. Prices had settled nearly $3 higher on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked energy supply concerns. Brent finished the week up 6 per cent and WTI ended 2.3 per cent higher. Attacks continued over the weekend with Houthis saying they had attacked the Saudi airport and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The top oil exporter restarted partial operations at its main airport on Sunday after damage in a previous round of Houthi attacks even as the militant group vowed to keep targeting the facility.

Source: Reuters

Oct 26 : NEXTDC CEO Craig Scroggie will give up his fiscal 2027 bonus opportunities, the Australian data centre operator said on Monday, after it slashed its revenue forecast and paused future developments last week. Here are some details: • The company said the board has withdrawn the resolution proposing an approval of grant of performance rights and restricted rights to the CEO under the fiscal 2027 long term incentive plan. • Current Chairman Douglas Flynn has reaffirmed his intention to retire from the board once a new chairman is in place, after a short handover period.

• The board expects to appoint two new non-executive directors in the first calendar quarter of 2027, NEXTDC added. • The company said the board has also withdrawn the resolution seeking shareholder approval to increase the maximum aggregate annual remuneration of non-executive directors by A$300,000 ($210,660), with the incumbent non-executive directors also agreeing to an immediate voluntary 10 per cent reduction in their current fees. • Last week, NEXTDC said delays to electricity network upgrades at one of its major Melbourne projects would mean about A$140 million worth of contracted customer revenue this financial year would be deferred. • The firm is set to hold its annual general meeting on November 20. ($1 = 1.4241 Australian dollars)

Oct 25 : Elon Musk said on Sunday that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units, underscoring the soaring cost of building AI computing capacity.  Musk, in a post on X, attributed the successful debt raise to the company's investment-grade status and revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and launch businesses.  It was not immediately clear from Musk’s post what he meant by the deal being “closed” or whether investors had agreed to pricing for the debt. "This is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter," Musk said in the post.

For the fourth quarter, the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure, according to Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen. Reuters reported earlier this month that SpaceX was in talks with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion for the purchase of Nvidia artificial intelligence chips. The funding highlights the enormous capital requirement of the AI boom, as technology companies race to secure advanced processors and build out the computing infrastructure needed to support AI development. Musk said debt markets "have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers." As a result, he predicted neocloud companies would face significant consolidation and failures, and later said SpaceX won't buy any neoclouds, calling it “pointless.” Unlike larger cloud firms that serve a broad range of industries, neoclouds such as Nebius and CoreWeave mostly focus on tech customers and offer capacity tailored for AI technology. Investors have started betting against US neocloud and data center companies, after fears that their debt-fueled AI buildout was becoming unsustainable sparked a selloff. AI INVESTMENT, CHIP MANUFACTURING SpaceX's revenue climbed 161 per cent from a year ago to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI was paying off. The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink satellite internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service.  Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla in Austin, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year as it aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028.  Musk told investors in a conference call last week that a merger of his two companies would be "a good idea," citing growing overlap between them. Prior to its blockbuster IPO, SpaceX listed "manufacturing our own GPUs" among the substantial capital expenditures it is undertaking in its S-1 statement, warning prospective investors of its big spending plans to develop AI and other technologies.

Source: Reuters
